source.title: GrokAlign: Geometric Characterisation and Acceleration of Grokking
source.authors: Thomas Walker; Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun; Randall Balestriero; R. Baraniuk

record.tranche_reason: The study reports experiments on grokking using Jacobian and centroid measures and compares training interventions, rather than reproducing the original intervention.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported train/test generalization outcomes and time to a test-accuracy threshold. Jacobian rank, centroid alignment, robustness, and embedding Gini measurements are not rows because they do not themselves measure the versions' specified grokking behavior. Cited results from other studies are not extracted.
record.test_reason: Mostly a method paper: Table 1 and Figures 8–9 report how GrokAlign compares with other methods. One result bears on V3 and V5: in the MNIST grokking setup with large initial weights (Fig. 7), forcing input-Jacobian norms low gives generalization, while holding them high prevents grokking. A second result bears on V6: the authors state GrokAlign pushes a modular-addition transformer toward a classification-style solution instead of the algorithmic one (Gini proxy, Fig. 8).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors go further, claiming Jacobian alignment is the cause of grokking (under a low-rank Jacobian assumption). In their account GrokAlign induces robustness, inhibits or accelerates grokking, and dictates the learned solution. They attribute its failure to accelerate the trainable-embedding transformer to the model's natural algorithmic solution, which GrokAlign does not suit.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Jacobian regularization and centroid tracking, including MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments and transformer experiments based on cited pipelines; it does not reproduce the original grokking method.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects depend on loss function, Jacobian-norm constraint, and whether the transformer embedding and unembedding matrices are fixed. GrokAlign does not accelerate grokking in the transformer with trainable embedding matrices but does so when they are fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: Delayed robustness: centroid alignment rises at generalization and again at the onset of robustness (XOR, Fig. 4). GrokAlign brings robustness on sooner on XOR and CIFAR10 (Figs. 4–5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to input perturbations emerges with delay after generalization and coincides with Jacobian/centroid alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Centroid alignment is offered as a continuous measure that tracks the phases of generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-Jacobian/centroid alignment tracks the transition to generalization during grokking.

record.problems: Several relevant accuracy trajectories are presented only as figures. Table 1 reports relative accelerations rather than absolute steps or times, averaged across ten initializations. The experiments do not test the training-set-size relationship, and no uncertainty is stated for the figure-only outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant rows were left out. Other reported measurements, including Jacobian rank, centroid alignment, robustness, and embedding Gini coefficients, were excluded because they do not directly measure the specified grokking behaviors.

untested.parts: Neither the size of the delay nor its growth as the training set shrinks is quantified. The modular-addition runs report only GrokAlign effects.
Gradual circuit formation and later removal of memorizing components are not tested. Centroid alignment tracks test accuracy but is not shown to anticipate the jump.
Text and molecule data; a lazy-to-rich transition is discussed but not measured; the CIFAR10 delay is not described.
The efficiency comparison of circuits, a critical dataset size, and ungrokking.

missing.what: Solution type (algorithmic vs classification-style) under GrokAlign or fixed embeddings, inferred from embedding/unembedding Gini coefficients
Delayed generalization on XOR cluster data under weight decay, with centroid alignment tracking memorization then generalization
Final test accuracies for baseline, GrokAlign and adversarial training (88.9/91.8/88.0% and 86.8/88.2/87.8%)

record.verdict_notes: Most rows (Table 1, Figs. 8–9) measure the study's own regularizer against other methods, so they are unlinked. All grokking-relevant evidence is figure-only, with no numeric trajectories. The V6 verdict rests on an indirect proxy (Gini coefficients). The text says 6.31× where Table 1 says 6.41×. The adversarial-training time entry (↑1.92 ±0.29) is identical across both losses.

versions.untested_parts: The training-set-size relationship is not tested. The experiments do not report numerical train/test accuracy trajectories that establish the full chance-to-near-perfect pattern.
The study tracks centroid alignment and its relation to generalization, but does not test gradual formation of a generalizing algorithmic circuit or later removal of memorizing components.
The reported settings include MNIST and CIFAR10, but do not test text or molecule data or establish a lazy-to-rich transition. The CIFAR10 test-accuracy outcome is not described in the text.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning experiment is reported.
The study tests Jacobian-norm regularization and constraining Jacobian norms, but not the efficiency account, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits as causes of grokking.
